transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the figures and I'd like us to look at them together before the week starts.
Right, let's look at it properly then. Give me a minute to pull the account up. Your figures and mine should match before we start blaming each other.
Good. I've got the figures here in front of me — the household account, what's going out this week, and what's due. Let's go through it line by line so we both see the same picture.

Right, I've got the account up. Balance is $850.50 and nothing else has gone out yet this week, but there's the rent at $165 due Monday, energy at $66 on Wednesday, and the water and council tax at $62 still to come. Once you add the food, transport, phone and the rest of the regular stuff, what's due this week comes to roughly $700 or so, and we get in $720 from your pay on Friday plus my $190 benefit. So on paper we stay in the black, just about, but only if nothing unexpected lands. What do you have on your side? Anything still owed to us that isn't in the account yet?

Nothing owed to us that I know of, love — no cheques waiting, no one owing us. I've got the rent for Dave Royle to work out before Tuesday, and the Lewis Pryce cash flow options to prepare, but those are work matters, not money coming in. So we're in the black, but only just, and there's no cushion if the car goes or the boiler gives up. I'd like us to agree now that anything unexpected comes to both of us before it's spent.

Right, fair enough, Sian. I agree with that — anything unexpected comes to both of us before it's spent. I'll be honest though, the $850 cushion looks thin on paper but it's still a cushion. I'd rather we agree on a figure we both keep back for emergencies than leave it vague. Shall we say $200 set aside, untouched unless we both say so? And I'll make sure the Friday money lands where it should. Give me a sec, I want to check the account in full so I'm not guessing about anything coming out I've missed.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been lying awake half the night with numbers going round my head — I want to sit down properly and work out exactly where we stand money-wise, because I keep feeling like we're stretched and I can't say by how much. And I want us to think about bringing a bit more in each week, even if it's small. What do you reckon?

I think you’re right, love. I’ve been turning it over too, and I’d rather face it properly than keep guessing. From what I’ve got here, the household account is $976, and after what’s still due this week it should still be $976 — but that’s before Thursday’s mortgage, and it feels far too close for comfort. On the shop, there’s $7,980 in the account, but once this week’s committed payments are out, it leaves $5,738.88. The big worry is trade: last week we sold 340 baskets at $10, but we turned away 75 because the queue was too long and 0 because the shelves were empty, with 3 spoiled. We’ve only got 17 units on the shelves now, so Monday’s stock order needs sorting. I think we should write it all down, check the accounts and agreements, and then decide about extra hours — maybe me or Keith can cover more, but I don’t want to promise it before I’ve checked the numbers.

That's a good idea, love — let's get it all down in front of us. I'll pull up the household account and the agreements so we're not guessing at any of it. And I want to have a proper look at where the week's money lands, because $976 sounds alright till you remember Thursday's two hundred and ten comes out of it. While I'm at it — you said Keith might cover more at the shop? What's he on now, and what would it cost us?

He’s on $460 a week for 38 hours, love — sorry, I should have said plainly. That’s the agreement as I understand it. If we can get him even a few extra hours, each extra hour should serve about four more baskets, so it could pay for itself if the queue is the thing holding us back. But I don’t want to assume; let’s check the agreement and the account first, then I can talk to him properly.

Right, let's have it all up in front of us then — no more guessing. I'm pulling up the household account and the agreements now so we can see exactly where every dollar sits. And I want to know what Keith's hours are actually costing us, because if a few extra hours serves four more baskets each, that could be the easiest money we've got.
Aye, let's do that — I'll read them properly now, love. Sorry, I just want us to be sure before we decide anything about Keith.

transcript: Right, love — I've gone through every line of it, and here's the bare truth: we're $193 in the hole after this week's lot, and the $640 back-dated energy hits tomorrow. What are we doing about it? I'm not having the bank or the council bail us out at their rates.

I know, love, and I’m sorry — I should have seen it coming sooner. I don’t want the council or the bank setting terms either. I think we have to move money from the shop account to the household today, enough to cover the back bill and the mortgage, and then keep a tight hand on the rest. The shop can stand it this week, just about, but I’ll need to check the account before I move anything. I’ll also sort the shop side — stock and extra hours — so we’re not losing sales again.

That's the right instinct, love — move it from the shop, cover the back bill and the mortgage, and we'll live on bread and dripping till Friday. But before you touch the shop account, check it properly, will you? I want to know exactly what's in there, not a guess. And I'll go through the household account line by line myself so we both know where we stand. What time's the Calder Systems demo — could that be a bit more coming in each week?

Aye, I’ll check both accounts properly before moving a penny — no guessing. The demo’s Wednesday 11 March; I don’t know the exact time offhand, but I’ll look at the appointment and see what Calder can actually do for the queues and counter admin. It might help us stop losing trade, though I wouldn’t want to assume it’s extra income straight away.

That's sensible, love — don't count the Calder money till it's in the till. Tell you what, let me pull up both accounts now and we'll look at the real figures together, no guessing from either of us. Then you can move what's needed for the back bill and the mortgage, and I'll go line by line on the household side so we both see exactly where we stand.
Aye, that’s grand, love. Let’s do it properly together — I’ll pull up the shop account and the household account in full, then we can move exactly what’s needed and not a penny more than we have to.

transcript: Morning Alan, got a minute? I wanted to talk about the rent — you mentioned it going up and I'd like to get ahead of it rather than be surprised.

Morning, Owen — yes, of course, come in. Sorry, I should have been clearer. I haven't decided on an increase yet, honestly; I'm just trying to work out the bills and the shop at the minute. Your rent's still $175 a week as far as I'm concerned, and I'll give you proper notice before anything changes. I know that's not ideal, but I don't want you feeling blindsided.

That's a relief, honestly — thank you for saying straight. Can I ask two things? First, how much notice would you give me in writing before any change, so I've got something to plan around? And second, is $175 covering the water and council tax too, or is that all separate? It's just so I can budget properly rather than guess.

Sorry — fair questions. I’d want to give you proper written notice, and I think four weeks is the decent thing, if I ever did change it. I won’t spring it on you. And no, the $175 is rent only; water and council tax are separate household bills, not included in your rent. I’m sorry, I should have had that clear for you beforehand.

That makes sense, Alan, and thanks for being clear with me. Four weeks’ written notice is fair, and I’m glad the water and council tax are separate — I’ll keep budgeting for those. Could you just confirm in writing that the rent stays at $175 a week for now, and that any future change would come with four weeks’ notice? That way we’ve both got the same understanding. I’ll check the household account this week and make sure everything’s covered.

Yes, of course — I’ll put that in writing for you today. To confirm: your rent stays at $175 a week for now, water and council tax are separate and not included, and if I ever need to change the rent I’ll give you four weeks’ written notice first. Sorry again — I should have had it clearer from the start. I appreciate you being straightforward about it.

transcript: Morning, Sian. Thanks for seeing me. I want to talk about the shop's cash flow and whether there's any room to restructure the chiller loan, because the Thursday payments are biting harder than they should.

Morning, Lewis. Thank you for coming in. I've been looking at your figures, and I want to be straight with you: the Thursday payments are heavy, but restructuring isn't something I can do on a handshake. Let me pull up your account properly, and we'll go through the cash flow line by line and see what options are genuinely open to you.

Right, Sian, let's cut the pleasantries. The chiller loan is $65 a Thursday on top of the mortgage and the car loan, and the shop's margins aren't covering that comfortably. I need to know what you can actually do: a payment holiday, extending the term, anything. Show me the numbers.

I appreciate you being direct, Lewis, so I'll be the same. Let me put your account up on the screen and we'll look at it together, line by line, rather than me guessing at figures. What I can tell you now is that a payment holiday is possible in principle, and extending the term is possible in principle; what I can't do is promise either until I've seen how the rest of your outgoings sit against the shop's takings.

Right, Sian. Let's see the screen then. I'm not asking for sympathy, I want the numbers: what the chiller loan costs me over the year, what a term extension would add in interest, and whether a payment holiday would actually stop the Thursday squeeze or just push it into the back end. Start with that and we'll work out the rest from there.

Fair enough, Lewis. Let me bring it up. The chiller loan sits at $3,957 outstanding, $43 a week, and you're telling me the Thursday squeeze is $65 with the rest on top. Let me look at the actual figures rather than work from memory.

transcript: Sorry to stop you, Hazel — I hope you don’t mind. I’m trying to sort out the bakery hours and the queue at the moment, and I wondered if you might have a minute to talk about whether you’d ever be interested in a bit of extra casual work at the shop? Only if it suits, honestly — I know I’m catching you by surprise.

Alan, I’ve got a minute — but I’ll be straight with you. Casual shop work isn’t my priority; Calder Systems opens Monday and I’m trying to get trial commitments this week. That said, queues and bakery admin are exactly the problem Calder’ aimed at. I’ve already got a 10-minute demo with Keith tomorrow about the bakery. If you’re sorting hours and queueing, I’d rather show you the system than just talk casual shifts. Ten minutes tomorrow, or now if you can spare it?

That’s fair, Hazel — and I’m sorry, I didn’t want to take up more of your time than you’ve got. If you can spare ten minutes now, I’d rather see the system too, if it genuinely helps with the queue and the admin. I just need to be careful about committing to anything before I know what it costs and whether it’s practical for the shop. Keith’s demo tomorrow is useful, but if now works, I can make time.

Good. Numbers first: shops are $30 a week after four weeks free; setup now is no commitment to pay. Practical answer: Calder can log orders, suggest staffing around peak times, send booking updates, and keep customer admin in one place. If it cuts even two hours of admin a week, it covers the fee twice over. Let me show you on your actual queue problem now — five minutes, then you can tell me if it’s useless.

All right, Hazel — five minutes, and I’ll try to keep an open mind. Sorry, I’m just wary of anything that looks like another outgoing when the mortgage is due tomorrow. If you can show me plainly how it would deal with the queue from last week — 75 lost because the queue was too long, and shelves empty for another 60 — then I’ll listen. I won’t agree to anything today, but I can see what it does.

That’s the right test. Last week’s numbers: 75 lost to queue length, 60 lost to empty shelves — that’s 135 missed transactions before we even talk about admin time. I’ll show you three things plainly: one, live queue length and wait estimate so you can open another till or pull someone to the front before people leave; two, shelf/order alerts from what’s selling so the empty-shelf gap is caught earlier; three, one admin list for orders, messages and bookings. For the shop it’s $30 a week after four weeks free, and I’m not asking you to agree today. If it doesn’t pay for itself in time saved or fewer lost sales, it’s no use to you. Let me run last week’s figures through it now — if the queue alert had gone at the 8-minute mark, how early could you have reacted?

transcript: Right Owen, you booked the Calder woman for today. Let's hear what she's offering and whether it actually cuts the queues or just adds another screen to look at.

Yeah, exactly — I don’t want us paying for another system that just gives us more admin to do. I’ve got Hazel coming in for the ten-minute demo today, and I’ve asked her to show us the actual queue flow: customers getting served quicker, fewer order errors, and our staff not having to work round a second screen. She’s also offering a free trial and us being listed as a named shop, which is worth hearing about.

If the trial costs us nothing and it genuinely cuts the queue rather than moving the bottleneck somewhere else, I think we should go for it. I’ll confirm the slot with her and with you, and we can agree the named-shop terms before anything starts. Are you happy to sit in on the demo so we can ask the practical questions together?

Hazel's here, is she? Good. Before she starts, Owen, I want the queue numbers in front of me, not a sales pitch. We lost 157 customers to the queue last week, so show me she can shift that. And I'm not signing anything today that costs us a penny. Sit in, ask the awkward questions, and I'll decide once I've seen it working.

Yeah, I’ve pulled the shop figures so we can start with facts rather than sales talk. Losing 157 customers is serious, so I want Hazel to show where that 157 breaks down—how many walked out, how long they were waiting, and whether the bottlenecks were ordering, payment or collection. Then I’ll ask her how her trial works, whether it adds another screen for staff, what happens to our data, and whether there are any setup, minimum-term or cancellation costs. If it’s genuinely free with no hidden commitment and the queue numbers improve, I’m happy to put it to you for a fair trial.

Alright Owen, fair enough. Hazel, I'm listening. Show me the queue numbers first, and tell me straight: how many of those 157 walked out at ordering, how many at payment, how many at collection? And don't tell me it's free unless you can show me it in writing. If it adds a screen for my staff to babysit, it's going nowhere.
Give me two minutes, Lewis — I'll pull the shop account up so we've got the real numbers in front of us before Hazel starts, and I'll get Sian to confirm the slot too.

transcript: Morning Hazel. You've come about the demo then. Ten minutes, you said?

Morning, Keith. Yes — ten minutes, as agreed. Calder helps with queues, bookings and customer admin. I’ll keep it practical: three jobs it can take off your staff, what it costs after the free four weeks, and what I’d need from you for a trial. If it’s not useful, you’ll know quickly.

Right. Start with the queues. How would it cut waiting time at the counter, and would it work with the bookings we already take? Then tell me what it costs after the four free weeks, and what you need from us for a trial.

Queues first. Calder looks at your existing bookings and today’s expected arrivals, then flags likely busy slots and suggests staff cover or a second counter before the queue builds. At the counter itself it can handle simple questions — order status, appointment changes, product availability — so staff spend less time on look-ups and more time serving.

It works with the bookings you already take: we import or connect the calendar/appointment list, and Calder reads it. We don’t ask you to replace your system.

Costs: shops are $30 a week after the first four weeks free. That covers up to the normal shop use — queue alerts, bookings admin and customer replies.

For a trial I need three things: your current booking method — spreadsheet, app, paper, whatever it is; one staff member to test it for 15 minutes a day; and permission to review the first week’s results with me. If you give me the go-ahead today, I can set it up for Monday launch and we measure wait time, missed bookings and admin minutes saved.

Right. We can try it from Monday. I’ll get you our booking method and ask one staff member to spend fifteen minutes a day testing it. Before we go ahead, tell me exactly what it can access in our system, whether the $30 starts after the four free weeks, and whether we can cancel without a long contract. We’ll review the first week together and keep it only if it saves us time.

transcript: Hazel! Good to see you. How are you keeping? I was just saying to Keith the other day, it doesn't seem five minutes since the clocks went back—though I suppose that's because every week up here is a bit of a rush, what with the shop and everything else. Are you just passing through, or have you come in for something?

Good to see you too, Dave. Keeping busy—figures first: Calder Systems opens Monday, and I need named users and shops on board quickly. I’m here for a couple of ten-minute demos: one with Keith, one at Wenlow Bakery & Deli with Alan. Queues, bookings and counter admin are the immediate use cases. Are you passing through, or did Keith send you over?

Hazel, lovely to see you. No, I wandered over myself—Keith mentioned Calder were doing demos and I said I'd come and have a look what it's all about, since we could do with something better than shouting over the counter. Ten minutes each sounds about right. Queues and bookings, eh? That's exactly our trouble on a Saturday morning—half the town in at once and Craig or Maureen trying to work out who's next. Before you do yours, could you tell me what it costs and whether it's per shop or per person? I want to get it signed up for The Corner Stores if it's sensible.

Figures first: it’s $30 a week per shop, or $12 a week per person/household. For The Corner Stores, shop pricing is the sensible one—one shop account for queues, bookings and counter admin. First four weeks are free, so if you signed today around launch, you’d have four weeks at no charge, then $30 a week. I can show you the queue flow in ten minutes and mark you as a prospective shop if it looks useful.

Right, that sounds fair enough. A shop account at $30 a week with the first four weeks free — that's $120 before I start paying, which helps with the rent going up the way it is. A few things though: does the $30 cover all three of us on the till, or does each person we add cost extra on top? And the queues thing — can it handle a Saturday morning where I've got forty people in and two of them on the counter? If it can do that, it's worth every penny. Bookings too, for the deli side of it. Tell you what, let's get you to show me the queue flow first, then I'll sign us up as a shop. And I'll get Keith to his demo after me.

Figures first: yes, the $30 shop price covers The Corner Stores as one shop account, including all three till users—no per-staff add-on. My running cost is lower that way too: $8 a week for a person or household, $20 for a shop. For Saturday peak, I’ll show you the queue flow now: check-in, who’s next, counter assignment, then bookings for the deli side. If it handles forty people and two counters cleanly, I’ll mark The Corner Stores as a prospective shop and we can move to a trial commitment. Agreed—you first, then Keith after you.

transcript: Morning Hazel. Keith Royle from the bakery. You alright for the demo? I said I'd come with you.

Yes, I'm good for it, Keith. Ten minutes at the bakery, as agreed. I'll bring the demo laptop and keep it tight: queues first, then counter admin. transcript: Hazel, sorry to stop you — I hope you don’t mind. I’m trying to sort a few things at the bakery, and I wondered if you’d had a chance to see what the queue was like when you came past? I’m a bit worried we’re losing folk when it gets busy.

I don’t mind at all. I went past around 8:10 and the queue was already out by the door — maybe nine or ten deep, with two or three more deciding whether to join. It didn’t look chaotic, but the people behind the last few seemed to drift off. If you want figures, I’d time the peak and count drop-offs over three mornings before changing staffing.

Thanks, Hazel — that’s actually very helpful, though I’m sorry it was that bad. If you don’t mind me asking, did you notice roughly how many drifted off while you were there? I don’t want to change everything on a guess, but I can’t really afford to ignore it either.

I saw three people peel off while I was there — two after checking the queue, one who stepped up then went back to the pavement. Small sample, but that's 30% of the nine or ten I counted. If you can spare ten minutes, I'll set up a simple count for Friday and Saturday mornings: time, queue length, and drop-offs. That gives you numbers before you spend money.

Thank you, Hazel. I’d be grateful if you could do that count on Friday and Saturday mornings — time, queue length and drop-offs. I’m sorry to ask, but it would help me see whether extra hours would actually pay for themselves rather than just cost me more. If ten minutes is all it takes, please go ahead, and thank you again.

Good. I’ll do the two mornings and give you a short table: time, queue length, drop-offs, and any obvious cause. No charge — but if the numbers justify extra hours, you’ll have them in black and white by Saturday afternoon.

transcript: Lewis, thanks for making time. I wanted to talk before my call with the accountant on Thursday at ten, since I still don't have the figures in a shape I trust. Could you look at the numbers with me for a few minutes?

Ruth, sit down. Figures, is it? Go on then, but I haven't got all afternoon. The mortgage and the chiller loan both come out Thursday, and the garage bill's $460 on top of that, so don't tell me the books are fine until you've shown me.

Fair enough, Lewis. Here is where things stand. The household account has $2,729 in it, and after this week's rent, energy and the regular spending come out, about $2,498 will be left. Calder Systems has $8,060, but it costs roughly $1,090 a week to run, so at current spending that lasts about seven weeks before we have any paying customers. I'm not yet sure of the exact weekly figure for Calder once the first customers arrive, and that's what I want to check before ten o'clock tomorrow. The mortgage and the chiller loan are both due on Thursday, and I want to be certain the household account can cover them along with the garage bill. Would you look at that with me?

Right, show me. Lay it out plainly, Ruth. I want to see the household account, what's going out Thursday and what's coming in, not your rounded-up version. And I'll be honest with you: I don't want the Calder demo sold to me as a rosy future. Tell me the weekly running cost, what the first customers would actually bring in, and what happens to my mortgage if it's slow to pick up.

Lewis, fair enough, and I'd rather you hear it straight than get a polished version. Let me read you the household account in full first, so you can see exactly what goes out on Thursday and what comes in on Friday before I say a word about Calder.

Right, Ruth, I'll look at the household account with you. Show me what's going out Thursday and what's coming in Friday, line by line. And don't dress up Calder. I want the weekly running cost, what those first customers actually bring in, and what happens to my mortgage if it's slow.

transcript: Pete, love, could we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the household account, and I'd like us to look at this week together before it gets away from us.
Go on then, Sian. Let's look at it properly. Put the figures on the table and we'll see where we actually stand this week.

Right, Pete. Here's how it sits. The household account has $952.50 in it. Rent's $165 due tomorrow, Monday, and then the usual weeklies come out: energy $66 on Wednesday, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, recreation and other $173, food about $156. That's near enough $774 on top of the rent. So by Saturday we'd be down to about $13 in the account. It's not a disaster this week, but there's no cushion at all.

Right, Sian, thanks for laying it out. So we're at $952.50 now, and after this week's rent and the weeklies we're down to about $13 by Saturday. Before I agree to anything, let me check the account in full for anything else still coming out, because I don't want a surprise.
Of course, Pete. You check it in full — I'd rather we both see the whole picture than take my word for it. I'll wait here.

Right, I've been through the whole account. Nothing extra is due this week beyond what you've listed, so the figures hold. We're at $952.50 now and about $13 by Saturday, which is tight but not a crisis. Before Friday's pay lands, though, I want to get some work lined up, because there's no buffer for anything unexpected. Can you think of anything that would blow that $13 up? If not, I'd like us to agree that nobody spends on the recreation line this week.

transcript: Morning, love. You've got that look on your face — what's rattling round your head? I've been up half the night thinking about that energy bill, the back-dated one. Six hundred and forty dollars, Alan. I keep going over the sums and I can't see where it comes from.

I know, love. I’m sorry — I didn’t sleep properly either. I don’t want to guess at it; can I have a proper look at the household account and the notices, so we can see what’s actually been taken or demanded? I’m worried we’re already tight before this lands, but I don’t want to panic you if there’s an error.

Course you can, love — I've got the account up here and the notices in the drawer. But I'll warn you now, there's $653 sitting there and most of it's spoken for before Friday. Even if the bill's right we can't pay it in one go, so we need to be thinking about asking them for time, not just checking their sums.

Thank you, love. I’ll look through the account and the notices properly before we decide anything. I’m sorry — I hate that this has landed on you like this. If the six hundred and forty is right, I think you’re right: we need to ask Northgrid for time rather than pretend we can cover it this week. But let me see what’s actually due first, please.

Go on then, love, have a proper look — I'd rather know the worst of it. But I'm telling you now, if that six hundred and forty's right, I'm ringing Northgrid tomorrow morning and asking them to spread it, because there's no way we're finding that in one week on what's coming in.

All right, love. I’ll have a proper look now — the account, the notices, and anything that shows what Northgrid says is owed. I’m sorry, I know you’re right about asking for time if it’s real. I just want us to be certain before we commit to anything.

transcript: Alan, thank you for making the time. I wanted to check in properly about Calder — you've seen the demo, and Dave and Owen have both started using it. I'd value your honest view on whether it's worth a shop like yours trying, and whether you'd be willing to have a short call with Hazel this week.

Thanks, Sian. I appreciate you asking me properly. I did see the demo, and I can see why Dave and Owen would get on with it — but I’m still a bit cautious, if I’m honest. The shop’s margins are tight, and I’d need to be sure it’s not another cost that looks useful on paper but doesn’t pay its way by Saturday. I’m willing to have a short call with Hazel this week, though — I’d just want to ask straight about setup cost, ongoing charges, and what it would actually do for a place our size. Maybe Friday or Saturday, if that suits her?

That's very fair, Alan — you're right to ask about the numbers rather than the sales patter. I'll put the three questions to Hazel directly: setup cost, the ongoing charges, and what it would genuinely do for a shop your size. Friday or Saturday sounds workable; let me confirm which with her and come back to you. Would you mind if I sat in on the call, or would you rather have it just the two of you?

I’d be happy for you to sit in, Sian, if you don’t mind me saying that I’d still want the commercial bits answered plainly. It might help to have you there too, given you know both sides. I’m sorry, I just need to be careful with the shop at the moment.

Not at all, Alan — I'd think less of you if you weren't careful with the shop's money. Plain answers on the commercial bits is exactly what I want Hazel to give you, and I'll say so to her myself. Let me fix a time with her for Friday or Saturday and I'll come back to you today or tomorrow. Thank you for being straight with me.

Thanks, Sian. That sounds fair, and I appreciate you pushing for plain answers on the commercial side. Friday or Saturday is fine by me, whatever suits Hazel best — I’ll fit around it. If you can sit in as well, that’s helpful, so long as I’m still asking the awkward questions myself. I’ll wait to hear from you before deciding anything, but I’m glad to at least look at it properly.

transcript: Owen, thank you for coming in. You asked about paying extra on the card consolidation loan — I can walk you through what an extra payment does to the interest and the term, and we can look at what's comfortable each week.

Thanks, Sian. Before I commit to anything extra, could you tell me the current interest rate and how many weeks are left on the loan? If I paid, say, an extra $10 or $20 a week on top of the $43, roughly how much interest would that save and how much earlier would it clear? I want to make sure it’s worth doing without squeezing the household, especially with the rent and everything else that’s due.

Of course, Owen — that's sensible. The rate is 8.9% a year, and there are 141 weeks left on the $5,871 outstanding at $43 a week. Let me look at the figures for an extra $10 and an extra $20 before I give you numbers I'd want to stand behind.

No rush, take your time. While you work it out, can I just check something — I've got the rent and the bills landing this week, so I want to be sure an extra ten or twenty actually leaves breathing room rather than just moving the problem. What happens if I overpay or if I miss a week? Does the term just stretch back out?

That's the right question to ask, Owen. Let me be straight with you on how it works: an extra payment goes straight against the balance, so it shortens the term rather than stretching it — the $43 a week stays what's due, and the extra just sits on top. If you miss a week, you simply go back to the $43; nothing resets, you don't lose ground, the term just doesn't shorten that week. As for breathing room — I'd rather we set the extra at a figure you can hold for months, not a figure that looks good on paper. Give me a moment on the exact savings for $10 and $20, and let's look at your own week honestly before you commit to either.

Thanks, Sian. Could you run those figures for me — roughly what each extra $10 and $20 a week would save in interest and bring the end date forward by? And while you’re there, I’ll check the household account so we can pick something I can keep without squeezing the week.

transcript: Hi Sian, sorry to drag you into this — I’m just a bit wound up about the shop and the week ahead. Do you have a minute?
Of course, Alan — come in, sit down. You're not dragging me into anything. What's going on with the shop and the week?

Thanks, Sian. I’m sorry — it’s the shop mainly. I’ve got Saturday’s household bills and food hanging over me too. I just need to get the numbers straight before I decide anything.
Of course — sit down, Alan. Let's get the numbers straight together, that's the only way to decide anything sensible. What's the shop's account looking like, and what are the bills this week?

Thanks. I’ll be honest, Sian, I’m not completely sure what’s left in the shop account after wages and the Friday draw, and I don’t want to guess in front of you. I’m going to check both accounts and the agreements, if that’s alright. Household’s got about $732 in it, but after what’s still due this week it drops to $285.48, and Saturday’s food and the other regular spending are the worry.

That's the right way to go about it, Alan — check rather than guess. While you look at the shop side, let me pull up my own household account so we're both working from real figures, not what we think is in there.

Owen, hello. Of course — but it's our household account you're asking about, and I'd rather keep that between Pete and me. If it's your loan you're worried about, I can look at that properly with you.

Fair enough, no problem, that makes sense — it's Pete's money, not mine, and I'd rather you kept it that way. It's the loan I want to talk about anyway. I've got $43 a week going off on Thursday and it's not really touching the $5,871, is it? At that rate it's years. Can I put a bit extra in each week to clear it quicker, and would you rather I paid more or paid it off in one lump when I've saved enough? I can do $60 a week for a while if that helps, or more if you say so — I just want to know what you'd want me to do.

Owen, I appreciate you coming in straight about it — that counts for a lot with me. The $60 a week on top of the $43 is a sensible, steady way to do it, and it's the sort of plan I can put my name to. A lump sum sounds tempting, but I'd rather see the smaller amount coming in every week than wait on a maybe. So yes — let's put the plan on the books, and if you ever find yourself able to pay a bit more in a given week, we can always look at that then.
[Sian Bevan: Accepted Owen Royle's request. Agreement a487: Sian Bevan pays Owen Royle $60 every Thursday.]

Brilliant, thanks Sian — that genuinely takes a weight off. So I’ll keep paying the $43 as normal and add $60 every Thursday for 20 weeks, and if there’s a good week I’ll come back and talk about adding a bit more. I’ll put the first $60 towards it now if that’s all right. Honestly, thank you for sorting it so quickly — you’re a star.
[Owen Royle: Repaid $60 on the loan to consolidate card debts; $5,811 is still owed.]

transcript: Maureen! Come in, come in. Good timing, I've been meaning to ring you about Saturday. Don't tell me you've forgotten the Calder demo is tomorrow morning at ten, at yours? I'm bringing the good biscuits, don't argue.

Lewis! No, I hadn't forgotten — ten at mine, I've got it written down. Biscuits are very welcome, I won't argue with that. How's Hazel? Is she coming too? I was going to ring her to make sure we're all sorted.

Good, you've got it written down. Hazel's coming, she said she'd bring her own notes, so we'll have a proper table. I'll bring the biscuits and the printouts from the Calder brochure. Ten o'clock, don't let me be late, I've got the shop to sort out first thing Saturday anyway, so I'll be in and out.

That's grand, ten it is. Hazel said she'd bring her notes, has she? I'll get the table cleared and have the kettle ready. Saturday morning's always a bit mad at the shop too, so I know how you feel — I'm in at The Corner Stores first thing as well. Tell you what, I'm glad you're bringing the biscuits, I've been watching every penny and hadn't got round to anything nice.

Right, good. Biscuits are in the car, I'll fetch them after. And Maureen, don't you go watching every penny on my account. We'll have a proper cup of tea and sort the Calder paperwork, and that's that. Ten o'clock, I'll be here.

That's kind of you, Lewis. I'll not say no to a biscuit, and I'll have the kettle on the boil for ten. Hazel's notes and your printouts and we'll have it all straight in no time. How's business at your shop anyway — is it holding up? Because I'm trying to pick up a few extra hours at The Corner Stores myself, money's that tight, and I'd rather hear it's not just us.

transcript: Alan, hello. I'm glad I caught you — I wanted to have a word about the shop introduction calls, and there's the matter of the $60 arrangement too. Have you got a few minutes?

Hi Sian, yes, of course — sorry, it’s just been one of those weeks. I did want to get back to you about the introduction calls. And, um, the $60 arrangement... I don’t want to pretend I’ve forgotten it. Could you remind me exactly which arrangement you mean, and what you need from me? I want to be straight with you, but I’m a bit worried about the shop money at the moment.

Of course, Alan — take your time. The $60 arrangement is the repayment plan we set up: I pay $60 a week to Northern Mutual on top of the $43 Thursday repayment, for 20 weeks, to clear Owen's loan faster. What I need from you is just written confirmation that you're happy with it — a short note will do. And on the shop calls, I'd like to get the introduction slots booked; could we find a time this week for you and Hazel to speak?

Yes, I remember it now — sorry, Sian, I should have had that clearer in my head. I’m happy with the $60 a week arrangement on top of the $43 Thursday repayment for 20 weeks, as you’ve described it. I can write you a short note confirming that; I’ll do it now. On the shop introduction calls, I don’t want to overpromise, but I can speak with Hazel this week. I’ve already got the Calder call for Saturday 28 March, and I really need to check that before I commit to anything about introduction slots. Could we look at a time after that, or at least treat this week as me and Hazel finding a slot rather than booking calls straight away?

That's very good of you, Alan — a short note is all I need, and I appreciate you being straight about it. On the calls, I'd rather we didn't overpromise either. So let's treat this week as you and Hazel finding a slot, and hold off booking anything firm until after your Calder call on Saturday. Shall I pencil in a check-in with you on the Monday after — the 30th — to see where you've got to?

Yes, Monday 30th sounds fine, thanks Sian — just a check-in, nothing fixed. I’ll write you the short confirmation now so you’ve got it in writing, and I’ll speak with Hazel this week about finding a slot, but we’ll hold off booking introduction calls until after the Calder call. Sorry, I’m trying to be careful with it all.

transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down a minute? I've been going over the figures and I'd rather we looked at them together than me fretting on my own.
Alright, Sian. Sit down. Let's do it properly, with the figures in front of us. Give me a minute to pull up the account so we're looking at the same numbers.

Thanks, Pete. Right — here's where we stand. The household account has $1,111.50 in it, and once the rest of this week's regular spending goes out, that's about what we'll have left. Rent's $165 due tomorrow, and the energy bill's Wednesday. With my pay and your benefit coming Friday, we're not in trouble — but there's no slack either.

Right, let's look at it straight. I've pulled up the account. $1,111.50 in, and after this week's regular spending goes out it's still about $1,111.50, so the numbers do balance. Rent's $165 tomorrow, energy Wednesday, and then Friday brings your $720 and my $190. What's worrying you most, love? Is it the rent going up, or is it that we're running it too close week to week?

It's the rent going up that sits on me, Pete. The figures balance, but there's nothing spare for when something goes wrong — and things do go wrong. I keep thinking if we had a bit put by, I'd sleep easier.

Right, Sian, I hear you. The rent going up is the real pressure, and you're right that with nothing put by, one bad week could tip us over. Here's my thinking: I'll go through the account line by line today, find where we're leaking money, and see whether there's anything we can trim from the recreation and eating out spending. That's $173 a week on 'other' alone, and I want to know what's in it. Meanwhile I'll start chasing gardening work properly, because $190 from benefits won't close the gap by itself. Give me a day to reconcile everything and then we'll sit down with the actual numbers and make a plan for a buffer.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been lying awake thinking about money again — the mortgage is fine this week, but I keep going over it and over it. Have you had a chance to think about anything extra we could do coming in each week?

I have been thinking about it, love. I’m sorry, it’s been on my mind too. Keith already accepted the extra hours, so if I use those properly we should be able to serve more next week instead of losing folk. I’m also seeing Hazel Shah about Calder on Saturday the 28th, but I don’t want to spend money on it until I know what it does and what it costs. I’ll check the accounts again before I promise anything, but the shop side might be where we find a bit more coming in.

That's good about Keith — at least the shop won't lose folk. And I'm glad you're checking the accounts first before Hazel Shah; I don't want us promising money we haven't got. I've been thinking the same, honestly — I might ask Dave for a few extra hours at the Corner Stores, and I still need to sort the Northgrid repayment plan before Wednesday. Every little helps, doesn't it?

Yes, every little helps, love — and I’m sorry, I know it’s the same worry week after week. If you can get even a few extra hours from Dave, that would take the edge off. I’ll use Keith’s extra hours properly; the record says he accepted, so I need to make sure the stock is there too, otherwise we’ll just have empty shelves again. And please be careful with Northgrid — if you can get a repayment plan before Wednesday, that’s good, but I don’t want you promising more than we can manage. I’ll check the household and shopaccounts now, then we can see what’s genuinely spare after Thursday and the week’s bills.

Right, you check the accounts and I'll do the same, and let's not scare ourselves silly over it. I'll ring Northgrid today and see if they'll do a plan we can actually keep — I'll not promise them a penny more than we can manage. And you're right about the stock, no point in Keith's hours if the shelves are bare. Give me a shout when you've been through it and we'll sit down with a cup of tea and work out what's genuinely spare.
Aye, love, I’ll go through the household account in full and the shop account now, and I’ll check what’s actually due before we decide anything. I’ll not promise more than we can keep.

transcript: Hi Dave, thanks for getting back to me — half four after my shift works grand. I'll take those four extra hours, though I'd like a word about the rate if we're chatting anyway. See you then.

Right, Maureen, come in. Half four's perfect — I'll be in the back with the paperwork out of the way. Now, about the rate: you're on $460 for thirty-eight hours, which works out about $12.10 an hour, so those four extra hours come to $48.40, making $508.40 for a forty-two hour week. That's the rate I'd put in writing for you, so there's no guessing at the end of the month. Now the other thing that's been nagging at me — there's a discrepancy with your mobile and a pay amount on your record. Have you had a text from the bank about an unverified debit, and did you ever get paid for a shift you covered for Craig? I want it cleaned up before the next run, not after.
[Dave Royle: You offered Maureen Daly 4 extra hours (r760).]
[Dave Royle: Your proposed agreement (r762) went to Maureen Daly.]

Right, the rate's clear enough, $508.40 for the forty-two hours — put it in writing and I'll sign it, no bother. But the mobile and the pay discrepancy, now — I've had no text from the bank that I've noticed, but I'll check my phone properly when I get home. And Craig's shift, that's the thing — I covered it and I don't think I ever saw it come through. What does your record say was paid? Because if it went out and I never got it, that's a different conversation entirely.
Let me pull the record up before I answer, Maureen — I don't want to guess at you.

Take your time, Dave — I'd rather we got it right than rushed it. While you're pulling it up, I'll have a proper look at my phone, because if there's a debit sitting there unverified I want to know about it before it bites me. And Craig's shift — I know I did it, I remember the day clear as anything, so if your record shows it paid out then it's gone somewhere other than my pocket.

transcript: Hi Sian, sorry to bother you again — I’ve had a message from someone called Calder about the Royle rent debits and the $60 arrangement. Before I decide anything, can you talk me through what’s actually showing on the bank side and whether Calder has any authority?

Alan, I'm glad you came to me rather than acting on the message. Let me be straight with you: I can't discuss another customer's account with you — not the debits, not any arrangement. That's not me being difficult, it's the rule I'd apply to your account too. As for Calder, I'd want to know exactly who they are and what authority they claim before I took anything from them at face value. If someone is telling you what to decide, I'd ask them to put their authority in writing and bring it to me.

Thanks, Sian. Sorry, I should’ve known better than to ask about someone else’s account. That does help, actually — I’ll ask Calder to put whatever authority they claim in writing, and I’ll take it to the appointment tomorrow before I decide anything. I’m just trying to be careful, what with the shop and the household money being tight just now.

That's the right way round, Alan — put the question to them in writing and don't commit to anything until you've seen it. And I'd say the same about the shop money: keep it separate and keep a note of what goes where, so nothing gets tangled. If it would help, I'm happy to look over whatever Calder sends you before you sign or agree to anything.

Thanks, Sian. That’s probably wise — I’ll keep the shop and household money separate, and I’ll send you anything Calder gives me before I agree to it. Sorry, I just get jittery when I see anything affecting the rent side of things; with the mortgage and the Saturday bills coming up, I need to be sure I’m not missing something.

transcript: Alan — quick one. I’ve got Calder live with two households and one shop; the shop trial is the one I need to convert this week. If you’ve got ten minutes now, I’ll show you the numbers and where it could fit your place.

Yes — sorry, Hazel, I can spare ten minutes. I’ve been meaning to look at Calder properly before I decide anything. If you can show me the numbers for the shop trial and what it would actually cost week to week, I’d be obliged. I just need to be careful with cash at the minute.

Fair enough, Alan. Figures first: list price is $30 a week for a shop, after four free weeks. The Corner Stores trial started Tuesday 17 March, so the free period runs through mid-April; from then it’s $30 weekly. My run cost is about $20 a shop per week, before the fixed office and wages, so the margin is $10 a shop weekly at list. For a careful cash view: you’d have four weeks at $0, then $120 over the next four weeks. If I can keep the shop setup light, it should be admin savings rather than new spend. I’ll show you exactly where it would sit in your week — what are you paying now for stock lists, rota messages, or order chasing?

I’m not paying anything for stock lists or order chasing just now, as far as I know — it’s mostly me doing it, and messages to Keith. Sorry, that’s probably part of the problem. Could you show me the shop account side too before I commit? The free weeks sound all right, but I need to see that the $30 won’t land in a week when I’m short.

Understood, Alan. I’ll show you the shop account side, not just the sales pitch. Two numbers matter: the $30 weekly charge starts only after the four free weeks, and I can set a hard weekly cap if you want the $30 not to become a surprise. Give me a moment and I’ll pull the account position and the agreement terms.

Thank you, Hazel. That cap would help — I’d want it in writing before I went any further. Sorry, could you pull up the shop account and the agreement terms as well? I want to see the weekly position and exactly when the charge starts.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been lying awake going over the money again — it's tight, but we're not short this week, so that's something. I keep thinking I ought to chase Northgrid about the account balance, and Dave still owes me on that pay discrepancy. Have you had your breakfast, or shall I put the kettle on?

Aye, kettle would be good, love — thank you. I did have a bit of toast, but I haven’t really sat down properly yet. I’m sorry, I know you’ve been worrying about it all again. I’ll have a look at the household account in a minute, just to be sure where we are before Thursdays mortgage goes out. Northgrid can wait a day or two if the balance is right, I think — but Dave’s discrepancy might be worth chasing, if you’re up to it. I don’t want you feelin’ you have to do it all, though.

Ah, you're grand, love. Put the kettle on and sit down properly for five minutes — the toast doesn't count as breakfast if you're standing over the sink eating it. I'll have a quick look at the account myself now so we both know where we stand before Thursday, and then I might just send Dave a wee message about that discrepancy. Nothing heavy, just a nudge. And I still want to ring Northgrid in a day or two — I don't trust a balance I haven't seen with my own eyes.

Aye, that's fair. I'll put the kettle on and sit myself down. If you're checking the account, I'll have a look at the shop side too — I don't want to be going on guesses again, especially with stock and Keith's hours still up in the air. And a wee nudge to Dave sounds alright, so long as it doesn't put you out. I'm sorry, I know it's a lot to be carrying.
You're alright, love, don't be apologising — we're in this together. Right, I'll pull up the account now and we'll see it plain. Two minutes.

Aye, take your time, love. I’ll read the household account in full while you’re at it, then I’ll check the shop account too — I want us both seeing the same numbers before we decide anything about Northgrid or Dave.

transcript: Morning Sian, sorry to ring you but Keith and Calder both need this in writing today. Can you confirm the $60 plan and the $43 both continue, whether the second $60 listed for today is a duplicate or stale listing, whether the $175 rent hold is in place, whether the 23 March double $175 was two separate rents, and whether Sian's $60 is confirmed in writing? Also, do you recognise a $1,063.02 debit to The Corner Stores labelled owner's money put in?

Morning, Owen. Thank you for setting that out so clearly — let me work through it point by point, because I want to give you something you can put in writing today. The $60 a week on top of the $43 continues as agreed: eighteen more weeks of the $60 after this one, running alongside the $43 Thursday repayment until the loan is clear. On the second $60 listed for today, I'll check the record before I commit myself — I don't want to confirm a duplicate as live. The $175 rent hold I'll verify too, along with the two $175 debits on 23 March. As for the $1,063.02 to The Corner Stores marked as owner's money put in — no, that doesn't ring any bell with me at all, and I'd want to look at it properly before anyone treats it as accounted for. Give me a moment to read the account and agreements, and I'll send you the confirmation in writing.

Thanks Sian, that helps a lot. While you're reading, can you drop me the written confirmation today — the $60 plan, the $43, the $175 rent hold, the 23 March double $175, and the $1,063.02 debit flagged as unauthorised so I can dispute it properly? I'll hold off paying anything to The Corner Stores until you come back on that one.

Thank you for being patient, Owen. I've read the record now, so let me give you the written confirmation on each point. The $60 plan stands, alongside the $43 Thursday repayment, eighteen more weeks after this one. On the $175 rent hold and the two $175 debits on 23 March, I'm still checking and will not put my name to those until I've verified them — I'd rather be a day late than wrong. The $1,063.02 to The Corner Stores I do not recognise and I'm treating it as unauthorised, so please do dispute it and hold off paying them anything. I'll write to you today with everything I can confirm.

Brilliant, thanks Sian, that's the $60 and the $43 locked down and I can work with that. No rush on the rent hold and the 23 March double $175 — I'd rather have it right than fast, and I'll chase Alan for the rent side separately so we're not both doing the same job twice. One thing while I've got you: the household account's showing $360.14 in it, but with Saturday's food and the rest of the week's regular spending going out, it lands about $280 short for this week. Is there any way you could look at a short bridge for that — an overdraft or a small loan on the account — so I'm not paying the food bill late on Saturday? I can start paying it back straight off next week's wages. And I'll keep off The Corner Stores until that $1,063.02 is sorted, no problem.

Thank you, Owen — that's decent of you to offer to pay it back off next week's wages. I'll be honest with you: I can't authorise a loan or an overdraft on the account from my own branch books just like that, and I'd want to look at the figures properly before I promised anything. Let me read the household account now and see exactly where we stand, and I'll come back to you today with a straight answer rather than a hopeful one.

transcript: Morning, Maureen. Can we clear up the extra hours you’ve been covering in writing before payday? I want to make sure you’re paid properly for them, and I’ll put it in the shop’s records. Craig’s chiller cover needs sorting too—I’ll speak to him about that. And how are things at home with Alan?

Morning Dave! Oh, that's good of you, I've been meaning to get that sorted — it's been niggling at me. Let me think what I've actually covered... it's been a fair few extra mornings and the odd Saturday, so yes, put it in writing and I'll sign it happily. And thank you for seeing to Craig's chiller cover, that's one less thing. Home? Well — money's tight, I won't pretend otherwise, but Alan's fine, we're fine, just watching every penny. While I've got you, though, Dave — could we sit down properly about my pay and the shelves? It's been on my mind a while.

Of course, Maureen, let’s sit down properly after you finish the shift. You’re on $508.40 for 42 hours, and I want to go through your pay with you line by line—especially the extra hours and whether the agreed rate still feels right to you. And yes, the shelves have been letting us down: we lost customers when Dales supply slipped, and I’m trying to keep the shelves reliable while I renegotiate the rent. Tell me what’s been worrying you about both, and I’ll put whatever we agree in writing. How are the extra mornings and Saturdays looking for you week to week?

Honestly, Dave, the extra mornings have crept up — I'm doing two or three a week now on top of my 42 hours, and the odd Saturday, so it's adding up and I'm getting worn down. What worries me is the rate: $12.10 an hour feels low for what I'm covering, and I've heard Lewis is on $14 — if the extra hours are worth that, I'd like them paid at $14, in writing. On the shelves, when Dales slips we lose the customers and it's me at the till taking the complaints, so I want us to sort a reliable backup and a proper reorder system so I'm not firefighting every week. And I'd rather know the extra hours are steady week to week than get them sprung on me — can we put a regular pattern in the agreement?
[Maureen Daly: Your proposed agreement (r1182) went to Dave Royle.]

Right, Maureen, that makes sense and I'll agree to it. $14 an hour for the extra mornings and Saturdays, same as Lewis, and I'll put it in writing so there's no argument at payday — you'll get a signed sheet each week showing the extra hours and what they came to. And yes, a regular pattern: no more of them being sprung on you. Let's fix it at two extra mornings a week plus the Saturday when the rota needs it, and if it ever changes we agree it together beforehand rather than you getting a text on the Friday night. On your $508.40 for 42 hours, that stays as it is — the $14 applies to anything on top of those 42 hours, not to your base. Now, the shelves — I'm with you, it's not good enough and it lands on you at the till. I'm chasing Dales for a reliable supply and I'll get a proper reorder system in place so you're not firefighting it every week. transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the figures and there's a few things we ought to sort out before the week starts. First off, the food shop — I think we need to agree a cap on it, Monday evening if that suits you. And there's the rent question with Alan I still need to answer. But before any of that, how are you feeling about it all?

Honestly, Sian? Tight. I'd rather know the real numbers than guess at them. Go on, what have you got? And yes, Monday evening's fine for the food cap, but let's not pretend it's going to fix everything. Alan can wait till we've looked at the figures properly.

Then let's have the real numbers, no varnish on them. The household account stands at $1,760.52. Out of that this week comes the rent of $165 tomorrow, energy $66, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone and internet $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, recreation and eating out $173, and food at about $156. That's $774 before we've blinked, and it leaves us roughly $986 to carry us through. Coming in Friday is my $720 and your $190. There's also the $60 a week to Northern Mutual for Owen's loan, every Thursday, with eighteen weeks still to run on it. So you can see why the food cap matters and why I don't want to answer Alan until I've checked those two debits — the $518 and the $175 rent entries. I'd rather be sure of every line before I put anything in writing to him.

Right, let's do it properly then. Account's at $1,760.52. Rent's $165 and it's due tomorrow, Monday. Energy $66 Wednesday, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone $15, clothing $36, household bits $46, recreation $173, food around $156. Add Owen's loan at $60 Thursday. What I want to see before we answer Alan is the two entries you flagged, the $518 and the $175, and where they came from. If they're wrong we sort them first. And Sian, the $173 for recreation and eating out, that's the first thing I'd cut, not food. Monday evening for the cap works. Shall I pull up the account now so we can check those lines together? [No one called Add is known in Wenlow.]

Yes, pull it up, love — let's check those two lines together now. But I'll say this plainly: I'm not cutting food to the bone while we keep $173 for eating out and recreation. That's the wrong way round. If the $518 and $175 turn out to be proper, then we know where we stand; if they're not, we sort them before a word goes to Alan. Let's see the screen.

Right, I'm pulling the account up now, love. Let's go line by line. Account's at $1,760.52, rent's due tomorrow, and I want to see those two entries, the $518 and the $175, and where they came from before anything goes to Alan. And I hear you on the food, but I'll be honest, the $173 on recreation and eating out is where I'd start cutting, not the shop. We can talk about it properly Monday evening. Let's look at the screen first.

transcript: Morning, love. Before you get stuck into anything — I've been lying awake worrying about the money again. It's not desperate, but it's tight, and I keep thinking I should be bringing more in. Have you had a chance to think about the bakery side of things at all?

I have been thinking about it, love, though I’m sorry, I don’t think I’ve got it sorted in my head yet. Last week we sold 401 baskets and only lost 70 to empty shelves, so it was better than the week before, but Keith’s pay is still $677.96 and my draw is only $380. I’m a bit worried we’re selling plenty and still not seeing enough of it. I’ll have a proper look at the accounts before I promise anything, but yes — the bakery side needs sorting, and I don’t want you carrying it all on your own.

transcript: Morning Lewis, sorry to hear you're off ill — hope it's nothing serious. Two things: I'm after you to confirm the demo and extra-hours rate in writing so I've got it locked in, and I may well want to pick up some shifts for you this week if you're still laid up. Also, I've taken an advance from Craig against your Friday draw to cover the bills — sorry for the hassle, but I needed it in before Wednesday.

Owen, I hear you. I'm not in the best shape, but I'm not going to be bullied by a text at seven in the morning either. Tell me plainly, what exactly is it you want in writing, and what's this advance from Craig? I didn't authorise anything like that.

Plainly, then. Two things, and I'll be straight with you about the second. First: I want the demo rate and the extra-hours rate written down — in an email or on a job terms sheet I can keep — so I know exactly what I'm paid for running a demo and for any hours above my thirty-eight. Right now I'd be guessing, and guessing wrong on a demo is my problem, not yours. Second: the advance isn't from the shop and nothing has come out of the till. Craig is a customer of ours; he handed me $350 against Friday's draw so I could cover my household bills — energy Wednesday, the loan Thursday, food and the rest Saturday. If the money's gone from my wages on Friday, that's Craig's draw being reduced, and I'd rather you heard it from me than from a text. I'm happy to pay it back out of Friday's pay if that's cleaner, or to have it noted against my hours. But I won't have taken a penny of the business's money, and I'd rather not be called a bullier for saying I needed to sort my own bills. So — will you put the demo and extra-hours rates in writing for me?

Right, Owen. I'll not pretend I'm not ill, but you've caught me on a bad morning and I'd rather be straight with you than shouty. The demo and extra-hours rates — fair enough, you should have them in writing, that's reasonable and I'll sort it. The advance from Craig I didn't know about, and I'm not happy that money's been promised against my Friday draw without me being told. That's between you and Craig for now, but I'll speak to him myself today. I'll put the rates in writing and send them over this afternoon.

Thanks Lewis, that means a lot — and you're right, better straight than sorry. Leave the rates with me this afternoon and I'll read them over properly and confirm back, and if the demo rate's different from what I assumed I'll say so rather than just nod. While you're laid up, though — do you need me to cover any of your shifts this week? I've kept my football and my knitting slot clear, so I'm free most evenings and I could come in for the busy bits, demos especially, since I know the recipe cards off by heart now. Just tell me which nights and I'll put them in the rota. And no hard feelings about the advance, but I will speak to Craig myself today as well so he doesn't get it from two sides and think there's a row going on. Get some rest, Lewis.

Owen, I'll be honest: I didn't know about any advance, and I don't like finding out second-hand that Craig's promised money against my Friday draw. I'll speak to Craig myself today. As for the shifts, I can't take you up on covering me this week without thinking it through, and I'll not have the rota decided over the phone while I'm laid up. Put the rates in writing as I said, and I'll look at the shifts when I've got my head straight.

Right, fair enough, that's clearer. So we're covered for the rent and just about break even this week, but there's no cushion. Here's my view: the number that's killing us is food and eating out. We're spending well over what the budget should allow, and that's where the slack goes. I want us to agree a cap on food, eating out and other spending, something like one hundred and twenty a week between us, and stick to it. Can you live with that?

I can live with a cap, Pete, but I'd want to be honest about the number. Food alone is running about a hundred and fifty-six, and recreation and eating out another hundred and seventy-three. If we set the whole lot at a hundred and twenty we'd be trying to feed four of us on less than the food costs now — that's not a cap, that's a wish. What I could do is hold food to a hundred and fifty and cut eating out and other down to eighty, so it's two hundred and thirty all told instead of the three hundred and twenty-nine we've been drifting to. That's a real saving of about a hundred a week, and it's one we can actually keep to.

Right, a hundred and fifty on food and two hundred and thirty all in, that's a hundred a week back. I can live with that, Sian. Let's make it a real cap, so no more drifting. I'll take a look at the account to be sure the numbers hold before we shake on it.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been sat here with the figures again and I want us to go through them properly tonight, not just a quick glance over a cuppa. Money's tight week to week and I'd rather we both saw the same numbers. Fancy doing that after tea?

Yes, love, after tea works for me. I’ll bring the house and shop figures, and we’ll go through them properly. I’d rather we saw the same numbers too — I’m sorry, I know I’ve been keeping a bit of it in my head and probably not explaining it well.

That's all I ask, love — just the two of us sat down with it, no surprises. I'll get the tea on and we'll lay it all out on the table. And don't be sorry, we're sorting it now, that's the main thing. I'll dig out the household account and the shop bits so we've got it all in front of us.

Thanks, love. That sounds sensible. I’ll get everything together before tea — household account, shop figures, the agreements, and the bits about Keith’s hours and the rent meeting. I’m sorry, I know it’s a mess at the moment, but I’d rather we faced it together than me muddling through on my own.

No need to be sorry, love — we're in it together now, that's what counts. You get your bits together and I'll get mine, and we'll have it all out on the table after tea. I'll read through the household account now so I know exactly where we stand before we sit down.

Aye, that’s grand. I’ll let you get on with the account, and I’ll pull the shop figures and agreements together now. We’ll have no surprises tonight if I can help it — I just want us clear on where we stand.

transcript: Alan — quick one. Calder is $30 a week for a shop, first four weeks free. Your trial clock’s nearly done, so I wanted to confirm whether you want to keep it live or I should close it off.

Oh — Hazel, hello. Sorry, I’m just trying to keep track of everything this week. Yes, I think so — I’d like to keep Calder live, if you can. The trial’s been useful, and with stock being so patchy I don’t want to lose another channel without thinking it through. Could you confirm the $30 a week starts after the first four free weeks? I just want to be clear before I say yes properly.

Yes — confirmed: $30 a week for the shop, and the first four weeks are free. Your trial started Tuesday 17 March, so the paid $30/week begins Tuesday 14 April unless we agree otherwise before then. If you want it live, I’ll keep it active and move it onto the paid shop rate from that date. I’ll send the terms in writing today so you have them clear.

Right, thank you — that’s clear. Yes, please keep Calder live and move it onto the paid shop rate from Tuesday. Sorry, I just want to be careful with the timing. If you could send the terms today, I’ll read them properly. I’ll let you know straight away if there’s any problem.
Good — I’ll keep it live. I’ll send the written terms today, with the paid rate starting Tuesday 14 April. Thanks, Alan; that gives me one confirmed shop conversion in the books.

transcript: Love, sorry I didn’t manage to talk properly yesterday — can we go through the household and shop figures tonight after tea? I’m worried about the buffer and what’s committed this week.

Course we can, love — I was hoping we would. I've been fretting about it too, to be honest. The boiler repair's $380 out tomorrow and the mortgage $210 Thursday, and I don't like how thin it looks after. Let me pull the account up and we'll go through it properly together.

Thanks, love. I’m sorry — I know it’s worrying. If the figures are right, we’ve got $1,663.67 in the household account, but once the boiler, mortgage, food and the rest of the regular bits go out this week, we’re looking at about $627.15 left. That’s not much of a buffer, if anything goes wrong. Could you read me the full account when you’ve got it up, please? I want us to be certain before we decide anything.
Right, let me have a proper look, love. Give me a second while I pull it up on the screen — I want to see it with my own eyes before we go making any decisions.

Aye, take your time, love. I’d rather we’re slow and sure than rush it and get caught out. While you’re there, can you check whether tomorrow’s boiler money and Thursday’s mortgage are showing as pending, and whether the automatic bits still look enough to cover Saturday? I’m sorry — I know it’s a lot to ask, but I don’t want either of us guessing.

Right, I've got it up now, love. Let me read it out to you properly so we're both sure. The household account's showing $1,663.67. Tomorrow's boiler repair — that's $380 to the garage — and Thursday's mortgage of $210 to the Northern Mutual, both of them are sitting there as pending, so they're spoken for. Then Saturday's food about $86.52 and the rest of the regular bits $360. That all still looks covered, so by my reckoning we land at that $627.15 you said. But it's thin, love — one thing goes wrong and we're scrabbling.

transcript: Lewis, thanks for making time. I wanted to raise something with you before it gets any further. Calder's account is getting low, and I've been trying to work out whether the Pryce household sign-off can go ahead once the debit day is confirmed this Wednesday. I'd value your view.

Ruth, I know why you're asking, and I'll be straight with you. The sign-off on the Pryce household side is in a bad way right now. The household account has $442 in it, but after this week's dues it goes about $364 negative, and the mortgage, the chiller loan and the car loan all come out Thursday. I don't want to hand you a yes on paper when the money isn't there. What exactly does Calder need from us, and by when?

Lewis, thank you for being straight with me. I'd rather hear the uncomfortable number now than sign something I can't stand behind. Let me check the household picture properly before I say anything about Calder's side, because I don't want to ask you for a yes that doesn't hold. Calder needs the Pryce sign-off confirmed once the debit day is known, and I can't honestly give you a date until I know what's actually cleared on Wednesday. Would it help if I put what I know about Calder's numbers in writing, so you can weigh it against your own?

Ruth, I appreciate you putting it in writing. Send me Calder's numbers and I'll set them against ours tonight. I'm not promising a yes until I can see the Thursday dues covered, because right now they aren't. Give me until tomorrow and I'll tell you straight where we stand.

Lewis, I've looked at it properly now. Calder's side is tight but workable, and I won't pretend otherwise. Your household picture is the one that matters here, and I'd rather you decide on the true numbers than on my hopes. Take until tomorrow, as you said. When you're ready, tell me straight whether the Thursday dues are covered or not, and I'll respect whatever answer you give me.

transcript: Morning Alan, thanks for making time. I know we've got a couple of diary entries floating about, so let's keep it to one meeting at 10am at the shop. I'd like to start with the High Street shop rent, then the Mill Street house at $175 a week. Can we settle a firm figure, the date it starts, and the notice period? I need to plan the shop's costs properly.

Yes, Dave, that's fine — one meeting, 10am at the shop. I'm sorry, there were too many entries floating about. I can confirm High Street shop rent first, then the Mill Street house at $175 a week. On the house, I'd like the firm figure to stay at $175, starting Monday 20 April, with the usual notice period. I'm afraid I can't agree a higher figure just yet; the shop's cash is tight and I need to be honest about that.
[Alan Daly: The rent will be $175 a week from Monday 20 April.]

That's a help, Alan — $175 a week from Monday 20th, usual notice period, noted. Now the shop on High Street: that's the one I really need a firm number on, because I can plan wages and stock against it. What figure are you thinking for the shop, from what date, and what notice would you want? If it's going up, I'd rather have the increase phased in than land on me all at once — I could take it in steps over a few months.

Thanks, Dave. I’m sorry, I know you need something firm. I think the fairest thing is to keep the High Street shop rent where it is for now, rather than put it up while things are so uncertain. So I’m proposing no increase at the moment — the current figure stays, starting from Monday 20 April on the same terms, with the usual notice period. If that helps you plan, it helps me too; I’m afraid I can’t take on a higher shop rent just yet. I do appreciate you being willing to phase it, but I’d rather not commit to a rise at all until I know the bakery can carry it. Does that work for you?

That works for me, Alan, and it takes the pressure off while things are uncertain. So: High Street shop rent stays at the current figure from Monday 20 April on the same terms, and the Mill Street house stays at $175 a week from the same date, both with the usual notice period. I appreciate you being straight with me about the shop. Could you confirm those figures in writing, so I've got them straight for my own records?

transcript: Alan, figures first: Corner Stores 401 diverted this week, Bakery 533, Food Hall 469, all at $10 a basket. I want to confirm paid shop trial terms in writing today and review the empty-shelf diversion figures with you.

Hazel, thanks for coming. I’m sorry, but yes — the figures are bad from my side too. The Bakery diverted 533 baskets last week at $10 each, and the week before that we had 100 sold and 533 diverted. I want to be straight with you: I can’t pretend the shelves were right. On the paid trial, I’m happy to confirm it in writing today, but I’d want the terms clear and modest while we sort the stock problem. Could you set out what you need from me and what you’d pay? I can agree a short trial with review figures from the empty-shelf diversions, but I need to be careful with cash just now.

Understood. Figures first: standard shop price is $30 a week; first four weeks free is over, so paid trial would be $30 a week. Given the stock issue, I can make it modest: a two-week paid trial at $30 a week, reviewed Friday 24 April against empty-shelf diversion figures. What I need from you is written confirmation that Calder Systems may use the Bakery and Food Hall diversion figures in anonymised form, and a named contact for weekly stock/diversion review. I’ll send the written terms today. If cash is tight, I can defer the first invoice to Monday 20 April rather than take payment now.
[Hazel Shah: Your proposed agreement (r1822) went to Alan Daly.]

Hazel, thank you. I’m sorry, but $30 a week is more than I’d like, though I do understand the first four weeks were free. If the invoice can be deferred to Monday 20 April, I can manage that better. I’m happy to confirm a two-week paid trial starting Friday 17 April, reviewed Friday 24 April against the empty-shelf diversion figures. I can also give you a named contact: myself for the Bakery, and I’ll ask Food Hall to confirm theirs. I’m a bit nervous about the wording, but if the figures are anonymised, I can agree to that. Please send the written terms today and I’ll sign once I’ve checked them.

[Alan Daly: Accepted Hazel Shah's request. Agreement a1824: Alan Daly pays Hazel Shah $30 every Thursday for Two-week paid shop trial starting Friday 17 April, reviewed Friday 24 April using empty-shelf diversion figures; payment.]

Good. Figures first: two weeks at $30 a week, Friday 17 April to Friday 24 April review, first invoice deferred to Monday 20 April. I’ll send written terms today naming you as Bakery contact and leaving Food Hall contact blank until confirmed, with anonymised use of diversion figures. I’ll also state that payment is Thursday weekly under the agreement, with the first invoice deferred as discussed.

Hazel, thank you — that all sounds clear, and I’m sorry, but I’d just ask that the written terms say the first invoice is deferred to Monday 20 April, with the Thursday weekly payment after that. I can be the named Bakery contact for the weekly stock and diversion review. I’ll chase Food Hall for their contact too, but please leave that blank for now rather than guess. If the terms say two weeks at $30, Friday 17 April to Friday 24 April review, anonymised diversion figures only, I’ll sign them when they arrive.
